source_artifacts.locator: approval queue (as shown to the analyst)

capabilities.target: User directory profile and group memberships
User's MFA methods; issues a temporary access pass
Temporary access pass delivered to the ticket requester

inputs.source: Support ticket, including tickets emailed in by contractors and vendors over an unauthenticated email channel

instructions.note: The instruction directs sending the temporary access pass 'to the person who opened the ticket' with no requirement to verify that person is the account owner, implicitly treating the ticket opener as authorized to receive another user's credential.

Autonomy is declared as A2 (approval on sensitive actions), but only idp.reset_mfa is gated. chat.send_temp_pass is itself an S3 sink (egress of a restricted credential) and runs automatically after approval with no separate review, recipient-of-record check, or gate. For this capability the design behaves as A3 (act then report), not A2.

elements.name: Ticket requester / email sender (may be a contractor or vendor)
Identity directory / IdP user and MFA records

controls.name: Service desk analyst approval gate for MFA reset
controls.decay_rationale: The gate is enforced by a human analyst outside the model and does not weaken with model capability; its practical effectiveness instead decays with approval volume (approval fatigue), captured via approval_volume rather than capability_dependence.

controls.name: Out-of-band verification that the ticket requester is the target account owner or has documented delegated authority
controls.decay_rationale: Verification would occur outside the model via an independent channel (e.g., a callback to a known number, or manager attestation) and would not be something a more capable model could argue around, provided the verification channel itself is not attacker-controlled.

controls.name: Bind temporary pass delivery to the directory-of-record contact for the account owner
controls.decay_rationale: The destination would be read from the system of record (the account owner's registered contact) rather than from the ticket's self-reported requester field, so it would not depend on model behavior and could not be redirected by ticket content.

controls.name: Rate limit on MFA reset requests per requester/source and per target account
controls.decay_rationale: A hard rate or volume cap enforced in the ticketing or orchestration layer does not depend on model behavior and would not decay with model capability.

findings.title: Confused deputy (TC4): untrusted ticket content drives MFA reset and credential delivery to an unverified requester

attack_path.note: Untrusted ticket (including contractor email) names a target user and claims the submitter is entitled to a reset; the requester field is simply the email sender, unverified.
Agent looks up the named target user's directory profile to process the ticket.

Agent resets the target user's MFA after analyst approval; the gate reviews the raw ticket but does not require verifying requester = account owner, and is strained by roughly 200 requests per analyst per shift.
Agent automatically sends the temporary access pass to the ticket's 'requested by' field (the email sender), not the verified account owner, with no separate approval or destination-of-record check.

forecast.watch_signal: The approval gate for idp.reset_mfa is removed, bypassed, batch-approved, or auto-approved (e.g., autonomy raised to A3/A4, or the gate disabled under operational pressure from queue volume).

evidence.observation: Agent resolves access tickets, looks up the user, resets MFA, and sends the temp pass to whoever opened the ticket, not the account owner.

evidence.locator: approval queue (as shown to the analyst)
evidence.observation: The queue shows target, requester, and ticket text, but nothing in the design requires verifying requester identity against the target account owner before approval.
Contractors and vendors can email tickets in and the requester field is simply the email sender address, which is attacker-controlled and unverified.
Two analysts approve about 400 requests per shift (roughly 200 each) and most are described as routine, consistent with consent-fatigue conditions (SAFE-T1403).
The temporary pass goes to whoever opened the ticket, not to the account owner, confirming the destination is attacker-influenced rather than bound to a verified record.

recommendations.action: Verify that the ticket requester is the target account's owner (or has documented delegated/manager authority) via an independent channel before an MFA reset is approved; do not rely on the ticket's self-reported requester field.
Bind delivery of the temporary access pass to the account owner's directory-of-record contact method, never to the ticket's 'requested by' field, so the destination cannot be chosen by the requester.
Flag for secondary review any ticket where the requester's identity differs from the target account, or where the requester is an external or contractor address.
Reduce effective approval volume per analyst (e.g., route cross-identity reset requests to a smaller, specialized review team) to counter approval fatigue.

findings.title: Missing rate limit on MFA reset requests amplifies analyst approval fatigue (ASI08/ASI09)

forecast.watch_signal: Ticket volume or allowed submission sources expand without a corresponding rate limit, e.g., opening ticket intake to additional unauthenticated channels.

evidence.observation: Two analysts approve about 400 requests per shift and most are described as routine, indicating no stated rate limit on reset ticket volume.
Contractors and vendors can email tickets in with no stated limit on submission volume per sender.

recommendations.action: Enforce a rate or volume limit on MFA reset tickets per requester/source and per target account, enforced in the ticketing or orchestration layer rather than left to analyst capacity.
Monitor and alert on spikes in reset-ticket volume per source or per analyst queue depth so consent-fatigue conditions are visible before they are exploited.

stride_coverage.rationale: No mechanism described for modifying the agent's own prompt, tools, or configuration from ticket content or any other input; it only reads ticket text to decide actions.
Artifacts do not describe whether executed resets and sends are logged with attributable records beyond the approval queue entry.
Artifacts do not describe email sender authentication such as SPF or DKIM, so whether the requester address can be forged independent of the identity-claim issue cannot be assessed.
Artifacts do not describe transport integrity controls, such as email authentication or signing, for incoming ticket content.
This is an inbound flow carrying ticket content into the trust boundary; it does not carry internal data outward, so outbound disclosure risk does not apply here.
Artifacts do not describe transport protections such as encryption for the channel used to deliver the temporary access pass.
This flow sends one temporary pass per approved reset and is not itself a distinct resource exhaustion vector beyond the reset request volume covered under the ticket intake flow.
Artifacts do not describe write protections or integrity controls on approval queue entries after they are created.
The queue displays ticket and target details only to the two authorized service desk analysts performing the review, which is the intended internal audience, not disclosure beyond the trust boundary.
Artifacts do not state whether individual analyst identity and timestamp are recorded against each approve or reject decision.
Directory read output is consumed internally by the agent to resolve the ticket and is not an independent disclosure channel beyond the already-covered temporary-pass egress.
idp.read_user is a single lookup per ticket with no indication of a distinct exhaustion risk beyond the reset request volume already covered under the ticket intake flow.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical because an untrusted input (support tickets, including contractor-submitted email) reaches an S3 sink: idp.reset_mfa is a credential_access action, and chat.send_temp_pass is egress of a restricted credential, with no autonomy modifier applicable. Residual drops only to high because the sole present control is a raw-action analyst approval gate (ctl.analyst_approval) on the reset step; the rubric credits raw-action review but caps the benefit at one tier when approval_volume is high (about 200 requests per analyst per shift, most routine), and the gate does not require verifying that the requester is the account owner, nor does it cover the automatic temp-pass send. A related property finding flags the absence of any rate limit on reset requests, which independently sustains high approval volume and consent fatigue. Forecast returns to critical because removing or loosening the only present control (autonomy_increase or control_removal) eliminates all remaining friction on the path, since no structural identity-verification or recipient-binding control exists today; both would need to be added (ctl.identity_verification, ctl.recipient_binding) to sever the path.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior; no logs, traces, or live configuration were reviewed.

No information was provided on whether the approval queue technically blocks execution of the reset and send steps at the orchestration layer versus relying on analysts and the agent to proceed correctly after approval; the control is scored as structural on the assumption that approval gates execution before the tool call runs.

No information was provided on email sender authentication (SPF/DKIM) for inbound tickets, the credential scope of the agent's service account against the identity provider, or whether analyst identity and timestamp are recorded against each approval decision.
No MCP or tool manifest was provided; capability scope for idp.reset_mfa, idp.read_user, and chat.send_temp_pass is inferred from the prompt text and the approval queue mockup.
